::: {.lead}
In fourteen lectures you built a toolbox for game worlds: positions and
vectors, the dot and cross products, distances and projections, angles with
sine and cosine, matrices, and the transformations that move, scale and
turn every object. Each tool rests on the ones before it: a transformation
is a matrix, a matrix acts on vectors, and a vector is the step from one
position to another (@fig-map). In this revision lesson you go through the
six parts once more. Each section gives the **key facts**, one **mixed
example** from a game, the most **common mistake**, and a short task. The
mini-game at the end takes you around all six parts.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary vector magnitude unit-vector dot-product cross-product projection unit-circle atan2 matrix-multiplication inverse-matrix rotation-matrix homogeneous-coordinates trs-matrix >}}

![The six parts of lectures 1–14.](images/course-map.png){#fig-map width=96%}

## 15.1 Positions and vectors (lectures 1–3)

::: {.callout-important title="Key facts 15.1 — Vectors"}
- A **position** is a point (x, y) or (x, y, z). Unity: x right, y up,
  z forward (a left-handed system).
- A **vector** is a step: B − A goes from A to B. Add vectors part by part;
  multiply by a number to scale them.
- **Length:** $|v| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 (+ z^2)}$. **Unit vector:** $v / |v|$,
  length 1, only the direction.
- **Motion per frame:** position += velocity × Δt.
:::

![Adding two vectors (lecture 3).](../week-02/images/vector-add.png){#fig-add width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.1 — The drone"}
A drone at (1, 2) must fly to (7, 10) at 5 units per second, at 50 fps.

1. Step: (7, 10) − (1, 2) = (6, 8). Length: $\sqrt{36 + 64} = 10$.
2. Direction: (6, 8) / 10 = (0.6, 0.8).
3. Velocity: 5 × (0.6, 0.8) = (3, 4). Per frame (Δt = 0.02 s):
   (0.06, 0.08). It arrives after 10 / 5 = 2 seconds.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Adding the parts to get a length: |(6, 8)| is 10, not 14. And moving by the
direction (0.6, 0.8) every frame without speed and Δt.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Vectors"}
1. A ship at (−2, 3) sails to (4, −5). Find the step, its length and the
   unit direction.
2. At 2 units per second, how long does the trip take?

*Your result:* a vector, a length, a unit vector and a time.
:::

## 15.2 The dot and the cross product (lectures 4–5)

::: {.callout-important title="Key facts 15.2 — Two products"}
- **Dot product:** $a \cdot b = a_x b_x + a_y b_y (+ a_z b_z) = |a|\,|b|\cos\theta$.
  A number. Positive: in front (less than 90°); 0: perpendicular; negative:
  behind.
- Angle: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{a\cdot b}{|a|\,|b|}$.
- **Cross product** (3D): $a \times b$ is a vector perpendicular to both,
  the **normal** of a surface. $x \times y = z$.
:::

![The sign of the dot product (lecture 4).](../week-02/images/dot-sign.png){#fig-dot width=90%}

{{< sim file="../week-02/sims/dot-lab.html" poster="../week-02/sims/dot-lab.png" title="Dot Lab: two vectors, one number" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.2 — Can the guard see the player?"}
A guard looks along f = (1, 0); its view is 90° wide (45° to each side).
The player is at d = (3, 4) from the guard.

1. f · d = 3. Positive: the player is in front.
2. |d| = 5, so cos θ = 3 / 5 = 0.6, θ ≈ 53°.
3. 53° > 45°: the player is **outside** the view. The guard does not see
   him.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using the dot product of vectors that are not unit vectors as "cos θ". The
dot product is |a| |b| cos θ: divide by both lengths first.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Dot and cross"}
1. In **Dot Lab**, find two vectors with a dot product of 0. What is the
   angle?
2. Compute (0, 1, 0) × (1, 0, 0). Compare with x × y.

*Your result:* two vectors, an angle and a cross product.
:::

## 15.3 Distance and projection (lecture 6)

::: {.callout-important title="Key facts 15.3 — Distance and projection"}
- **Distance** of A and B: |B − A|. To compare distances, compare the
  squared lengths (no square root needed).
- The part of v **along** a unit vector u: $(v\cdot u)\,u$. The part
  **across**: $v - (v\cdot u)\,u$.
- A wall slide keeps the part along the wall; a bounce turns round the part
  along the normal.
:::

![Projection: the part along and the part across (lecture 6).](../week-03/images/projection.png){#fig-proj width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.3 — Sliding along the wall"}
A player walks with v = (4, −3) into a floor with the unit normal
n = (0, 1).

1. v · n = −3. The part along the normal: −3 × (0, 1) = (0, −3).
2. The part along the floor: (4, −3) − (0, −3) = **(4, 0)**: the player
   slides right.
3. A bounce keeps (4, 0) and turns (0, −3) round: (4, 3).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Projecting onto a vector that is not a unit vector, for example (0, 2):
the result is twice too long. Normalize the direction first.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Nearest enemy"}
Enemies stand at (3, 4), (−5, 1) and (2, −2) from the player. Which is
nearest? Use squared lengths.

*Your result:* three squared lengths and one enemy.
:::

## 15.4 Trigonometry (lectures 7–8)

::: {.callout-important title="Key facts 15.4 — Angles"}
- In a right triangle: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$,
  $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$,
  $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$.
- A direction at angle θ: (cos θ, sin θ); with length r: (r cos θ, r sin θ).
- From a vector to its angle: **atan2(y, x)** (it knows the quadrant).
- 180° = π radians. Oscillation: $y = A \sin(\omega t)$.
:::

![The unit circle (lecture 7).](../week-04/images/unit-circle.png){#fig-uc width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.4 — Aim and fire"}
An enemy is at (−4, 4) from a turret. The bullet speed is 10.

1. Angle: atan2(4, −4) = **135°** (left and up). atan(4 / −4) would give
   −45°, the wrong way.
2. cos 135° = −0.71, sin 135° = 0.71.
3. Velocity: (10 × −0.71, 10 × 0.71) = **(−7.1, 7.1)**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using degrees where the code wants radians: `Mathf.Sin(30)` is the sine of
30 radians. Write `Mathf.Sin(30 * Mathf.Deg2Rad)`.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Angles"}
1. A cannon fires at 60° with speed 20 (cos 60° = 0.5, sin 60° = 0.87).
   Find the velocity.
2. Which angle does atan2(−3, −3) give?

*Your result:* one vector and one angle.
:::

## 15.5 Matrices (lectures 9–10)

::: {.callout-important title="Key facts 15.5 — Matrices"}
- An m × n matrix has m rows and n columns. Add matrices of the same size
  entry by entry.
- **M × v:** each row of M times v. **M × N:** row of M times column of N;
  the order matters (M N ≠ N M).
- **Identity** I: 1 on the main diagonal; I v = v.
- **Inverse** of a 2 × 2 matrix with rows (a, b), (c, d):
  $\dfrac{1}{ad - bc}$ times rows (d, −b), (−c, a). No inverse when
  det = ad − bc = 0.
:::

![A matrix times a vector (lecture 9).](../week-05/images/matrix-vector.png){#fig-mv width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.5 — Undo a spell"}
The spell M = rows (2, 1), (1, 1) sends a gem from (1, 2) to (4, 3).

1. Check: (2 × 1 + 1 × 2, 1 × 1 + 1 × 2) = (4, 3).
2. det = 2 × 1 − 1 × 1 = 1. Inverse: rows (1, −1), (−1, 2).
3. Undo: (1 × 4 − 1 × 3, −1 × 4 + 2 × 3) = **(1, 2)**: the gem is back.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Multiplying entry by entry. A matrix product uses rows times columns: the
entry in row 1, column 2 is row 1 of M times column 2 of N.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Matrices"}
1. Compute rows (1, 2), (0, 1) times rows (3, 0), (1, 1).
2. Does rows (2, 4), (1, 2) have an inverse? Why?

*Your result:* one matrix and one answer with its reason.
:::

## 15.6 Transformations (lectures 11–14)

::: {.callout-important title="Key facts 15.6 — Transformations"}
- **Scale** S(sx, sy), **rotate** R(θ) = rows (cos θ, −sin θ), (sin θ,
  cos θ), **translate** T(tx, ty).
- About a pivot C: move by −C, transform, move back by +C.
- **Homogeneous coordinates:** (x, y, 1) for points, (x, y, 0) for
  directions; 3 × 3 matrices in 2D, 4 × 4 in 3D.
- **M = T × R × S:** scale first, then rotate, then translate.
- Yaw in Unity: forward (0, 0, 1) → (sin θ, 0, cos θ).
:::

![The TRS matrix (lecture 13).](../week-07/images/trs-chain.png){#fig-trs width=90%}

{{< sim file="../week-07/sims/matrix-chain.html" poster="../week-07/sims/matrix-chain.png" title="Matrix Chain: M = T × R × S" height="820" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.6 — The flag on the tower"}
A flag is at (1, 0) in the local space of a tower. The tower is scaled by 2,
turned by 90° and placed at (3, 1).

1. S(2): (2, 0). R(90°): (0, 2). T(3, 1): **(3, 3)**.
2. One matrix: M = rows (0, −2, 3), (2, 0, 1), (0, 0, 1); M × (1, 0, 1) =
   (3, 3, 1).
3. The wind direction (1, 0, 0) on the flag becomes (0, 2, 0): turned and
   scaled, not moved.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reading T × R × S from left to right. S acts first, T last. And rotating
about the origin when the object should turn about its own pivot.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · One matrix"}
1. In **Matrix Chain**, build M for scale 1, θ = 180°, move (2, 3).
2. Where does the point (1, 0) go? Check by hand.

*Your result:* a matrix and one point.
:::

## Case study: Island Quest

*Island Quest* is a made-up revision game: a boat sails around six
islands, one for each part of lectures 1–14. On each island waits one
problem from a game: a drone's step and length, a guard who looks the
wrong way, the normal of two axes, a ball sliding along a floor, a cannon
at 30°, an enemy up and to the left, the inverse of a spell, and a point
and a direction under T(5, 1) × R(90°). The Game challenge of the
interactive lesson uses these problems. In the mini-game below you sail
around the islands.

{{< sim file="sims/island-quest.html" poster="sims/island-quest.png" title="Island Quest: one problem on each island" kind="game" height="640" >}}

## Further reading

Dunn and Parberry, *3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development*,
2nd ed., Chapters 1–6 (the summary at the end of each chapter).

## Exercises

1. A player at (2, −1) moves to (5, 3). Find the step and the distance.
2. Normalize (0, −4).
3. Compute (2, 3) · (−3, 2). What does the result tell?
4. Compute (1, 0, 0) × (0, 0, 1).
5. Which is nearer to the origin: (5, 5) or (−7, 1)? Use squared lengths.
6. v = (3, −2) hits a floor with the normal (0, 1). What is the slide
   direction?
7. A wheel of radius 2 turns 30°. Where is the point that started at
   (2, 0)? (cos 30° = 0.87, sin 30° = 0.5)
8. Which angle does atan2(1, −1) give?
9. Convert 90° to radians.
10. Compute rows (1, 2), (3, 4) times (1, 1).
11. Find the inverse of rows (3, 1), (2, 1).
12. Rotate (2, 0) by 90° about the pivot (1, 1).
13. Write T(−1, 2) as a 3 × 3 matrix and apply it to (4, 4, 1).
14. A tank has a yaw of 90°. What is its forward vector?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. (3, 4); 5.
2. (0, −1).
3. −6 + 6 = 0: the vectors are perpendicular.
4. (0, −1, 0).
5. Equally near: both squared lengths are 50.
6. The part along the floor: (3, 0).
7. (1.74, 1).
8. 135°.
9. π / 2 ≈ 1.57.
10. (3, 7).
11. det = 1: rows (1, −1), (−2, 3).
12. P − C = (1, −1); R(90°) gives (1, 1); + C = (2, 2).
13. Rows (1, 0, −1), (0, 1, 2), (0, 0, 1); (3, 6, 1).
14. (1, 0, 0).
:::
